title: Xanax and Alcohol: Why Mixing Them Is Dangerous
excerpt: Why Xanax and alcohol shouldn't be mixed: how both slow the brain and breathing, what the FDA label says, how long Xanax stays in your system, and the emergency signs to know.
metaDescription: Why Xanax (alprazolam) and alcohol are dangerous together: how they slow breathing, how long Xanax lasts, hangover anxiety, and when to call 911.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** don't mix Xanax and alcohol. This is not one of those interactions where a little is fine and only heavy use is a problem. Xanax (alprazolam) and alcohol both slow down the brain through the same chemical system, and together they can slow breathing, cause blackouts, and in the worst cases lead to coma or death. Most people who combine them once won't die, but there is no amount that is known to be safe, and the people who do end up in the emergency room rarely planned on taking "a lot." If you've been prescribed Xanax, the safest rule is simple: no alcohol on the days you take it, and talk to your prescriber about what that means for you.

**The quick rules:** Don't drink on a day you take Xanax, and don't take Xanax after you've been drinking, including the next morning if you still feel drunk. Never take Xanax to calm hangover anxiety. Never take a "Xanax" pill that didn't come from a pharmacy, because counterfeit pills often contain fentanyl. If someone has combined the two and is very hard to wake, breathing slowly or irregularly, or has blue or gray lips, **call 911 right away.**

> **This is not medical advice.** This article explains how Xanax and alcohol interact and what official labeling says. It is not a substitute for the doctor or pharmacist who knows your health history, and it does not give dosing advice. **Talk to your prescriber** about alcohol before you start Xanax, if you've already been drinking while taking it, or if you want to stop either one. **Call 911 immediately if** someone who has mixed Xanax and alcohol can't be woken, is breathing slowly, shallowly, or with long pauses, has blue or gray lips or fingertips, is having a seizure, or is vomiting while drowsy or confused. In the US, Poison Control is **1-800-222-1222** for non-emergency questions.

## How Xanax and Alcohol Interact: The Brain Chemistry in Plain Words

Xanax is the brand name for **alprazolam**, a medicine in the **benzodiazepine** family. Doctors prescribe it mainly for anxiety disorders and panic disorder. Other well-known benzodiazepines include Valium (diazepam), Ativan (lorazepam), and Klonopin (clonazepam). Everything in this article applies broadly to that whole family.

To understand why the combination is dangerous, you need one piece of brain chemistry.

Your brain has a built-in brake pedal called **GABA**. It's a chemical messenger that calms nerve cells down. When GABA attaches to its main receptor (called the **GABA-A receptor**), it opens a tiny channel in the nerve cell and makes that cell less likely to fire. More GABA activity means a quieter, slower brain. That's how you feel relaxed, then sleepy, then, at high enough levels, unconscious.

- **Xanax presses the brake harder.** Benzodiazepines attach to the GABA-A receptor at their own spot and make it respond more strongly every time GABA arrives. That's how Xanax reduces anxiety and panic.
- **Alcohol presses the same brake.** Alcohol also boosts GABA-A activity. On top of that, it blocks the brain's main "accelerator" chemical, glutamate. So alcohol both pushes the brake and eases off the gas.

When you take both, you're pressing the same brake pedal with two feet. The effects don't just add up neatly. They can amplify each other, which is why the combination can be much more sedating than either one alone, and why it's hard to predict how a given person will react on a given night.

### Why breathing is the real danger

The parts of your brain that keep you breathing while you sleep are also controlled by this braking system. At normal prescribed doses, Xanax alone rarely stops a healthy person from breathing. Alcohol alone at very high levels can. Together, the threshold drops. The two can slow breathing enough that oxygen levels fall, especially during sleep, when no one is watching.

Add vomiting to that picture. Alcohol often causes vomiting, and heavy sedation weakens the reflexes that protect your airway. Someone who is deeply sedated and vomits can choke or breathe vomit into their lungs.

### The liver plays a smaller role than you'd think

With many medication interactions, the main story is the liver. Xanax is broken down in the liver, mainly by an enzyme called CYP3A4, and alcohol is processed in the liver too. Some research suggests alcohol can change how quickly benzodiazepines are cleared, but that isn't the main reason this combination is dangerous. The main danger happens in the brain, at the same receptor, even if your liver is perfectly healthy. That's why "I have a strong liver" or "I have a high tolerance" offers no protection here.

## What the FDA Label and Official Guidance Say

Xanax's US prescribing information carries a **boxed warning**, the FDA's strongest type of warning. It's worth being precise about what it covers:

1. **Opioids.** Since 2016, the FDA has required a boxed warning on benzodiazepines and opioids saying that using them together can cause profound sedation, slowed breathing, coma, and death.
2. **Abuse, misuse, and addiction.** In 2020, the FDA expanded the boxed warning for all benzodiazepines to cover the risks of abuse, misuse, addiction, physical dependence, and withdrawal reactions.
3. **Dependence and withdrawal.** The same warning says that stopping a benzodiazepine suddenly or cutting the dose quickly after regular use can cause serious withdrawal reactions, including seizures, so tapering should happen under a prescriber's guidance.

Alcohol is covered in the label's warnings about combining Xanax with other **central nervous system depressants**, meaning anything else that slows down the brain. The prescribing information tells patients to avoid alcohol while taking the medicine because of the added sedation and risk. The same logic that led the FDA to put the opioid warning in a box applies to alcohol: two substances that slow breathing are more dangerous together than apart.

Public health agencies also track this problem. US government reports on drug-related emergency visits and overdose deaths have repeatedly found that benzodiazepines are often involved alongside other depressants, most commonly opioids and alcohol. Deaths involving benzodiazepines alone are relatively uncommon. Deaths involving benzodiazepines **combined** with other depressants are where the risk concentrates.

## Can You Drink on Xanax at All?

This is the question most people actually type into a search bar, and it usually comes with a hope attached: "Surely one glass of wine is fine?"

Here's the honest picture. Many people have had a drink while on Xanax and been fine. But "I was fine last time" is how dangerous interactions catch people. How strongly the two combine depends on things you can't easily judge in the moment:

- How much Xanax is in your blood right now, which depends on your dose, when you took it, and whether it's the immediate-release or extended-release (XR) form
- How fast you're drinking and whether you've eaten
- Your body size, age, and sex
- Whether you've taken anything else that sedates you, such as a sleep aid, an antihistamine like Benadryl, a muscle relaxant, cannabis, or an opioid painkiller
- Whether you're tired, sick, or dehydrated

Because no one can tell you a safe amount in advance, the official answer is the right one: **avoid alcohol while taking Xanax.** If you take Xanax only occasionally, "while taking it" means you need to think about timing, which the next section covers. If you take it every day, it means not drinking, and if that's not realistic for you, tell your prescriber. They would much rather know than prescribe blind. They may suggest a different medicine for anxiety that carries less risk with alcohol.

## How Long After Taking Xanax Can You Drink (and Vice Versa)?

There's no official waiting period that applies to everyone, and we won't invent one. What we can explain is how long the drug stays active, so you understand why the answer is "longer than you'd think," and why the question belongs with your prescriber or pharmacist.

**Xanax lasts longer than its calming effect.** The prescribing information lists an average half-life for immediate-release alprazolam of around 11 hours in healthy adults, with a wide range between people. A half-life is the time it takes your body to clear half of the drug. It takes several half-lives for a medicine to be mostly gone. So even when you no longer feel the calming effect of a dose, a meaningful amount can still be in your system well into the next day.

**Some people clear it more slowly.** Older adults, people with liver disease, people with obesity, and people taking certain other medicines (including some antifungals and antibiotics that block CYP3A4) can hold on to alprazolam longer. The extended-release form is designed to release the drug over many hours.

**Alcohol has its own timeline.** Your body clears roughly one standard drink per hour, with big differences between people. After a heavy night, alcohol can still be in your blood the next morning. Taking Xanax "the morning after" when you still feel drunk is combining them.

The practical takeaway:

- Don't plan a night out around "timing" a Xanax dose. If you know you'll be drinking, talk to your prescriber in advance about whether to skip a dose and how.
- Don't take Xanax after drinking until the alcohol is fully out of your system, and ideally not on the same day at all.
- If you take Xanax on a schedule, don't skip or change doses on your own to make room for drinking. Abruptly stopping regular benzodiazepine use can trigger withdrawal. This is exactly the conversation to have with the person who prescribed it.

## Taking Xanax for Hangover Anxiety: Why It Backfires

A lot of searches for "Xanax and alcohol" come from the morning after. You wake up with a racing heart, a sense of dread, and a replay of everything you said last night. Doctors don't have a formal name for it, but many people call it **hangxiety**. If there's a Xanax in the cabinet, it's tempting.

Here's why that's a bad idea:

1. **The alcohol may not be gone.** If you drank late or heavily, there may still be alcohol in your blood. Adding a benzodiazepine on top of it is the exact combination this article warns against.
2. **Hangover anxiety is partly a rebound from alcohol itself.** While you drink, alcohol boosts your brain's calming GABA signals and dampens excitatory glutamate. As it wears off, your brain swings the other way, which can leave you jittery, anxious, and sleeping poorly. Our guide to [hangxiety and what's behind it](/never-hungover/hangxiety-complete-guide-2026-supplements-research) explains this in detail. Using a second GABA-boosting drug to cover that rebound creates a pattern where you rely on one depressant to handle the after-effects of another.
3. **It can hide a problem you need to notice.** Shakiness, sweating, and a pounding heart after drinking are usually ordinary hangover symptoms (see our guides to [hangover shakes](/never-hungover/hangover-shakes) and a [racing heart after drinking](/never-hungover/heart-racing-after-drinking)). But in someone who drinks heavily every day, the same signs can be early alcohol withdrawal, which can be medically serious. Self-treating it with a borrowed or leftover Xanax isn't safe. That situation needs a doctor.

If hangover anxiety is a regular thing for you, the more useful fixes are the dull ones: fewer drinks, slower drinking, water and food, and sleep. Our article on [alcohol and anxiety](/never-hungover/alcohol-and-anxiety-breaking-the-cycle-naturally-2025) covers how the two feed each other.

## Blackouts, Memory Loss, and Risky Behavior

Benzodiazepines can cause **anterograde amnesia**, which means trouble forming new memories while the drug is active. Alcohol does the same thing at higher levels; that's what a blackout is. Together, memory gaps can happen at amounts of alcohol that wouldn't normally cause one.

That matters because a person in a blackout can still walk, talk, and make decisions. They just won't remember them. The combination is linked to:

- **Falls and injuries**, especially on stairs or in the bathroom
- **Drowsy or impaired driving.** Even if you feel only "a little relaxed," your reaction time and judgment can be badly affected. Don't drive after combining them, and don't drive the next morning if you still feel foggy.
- **Doing or saying things you wouldn't otherwise do**, because both substances lower inhibition
- **Taking more without realizing it**, because you don't remember the first dose or the last few drinks

There is also a safety issue for others. Sedating drugs mixed into drinks are used in drug-facilitated assault. If you or a friend feel far more impaired than the amount you drank would explain, get to a safe place with someone you trust and seek medical help.

## Counterfeit Xanax: A Separate and Serious Danger

Not every pill sold as "Xanax" is Xanax. US law enforcement agencies, including the DEA, have warned for years that counterfeit pills made to look like prescription medicines, including alprazolam "bars," are common in the illegal market and often contain **fentanyl** or other dangerous substances.

This changes the risk completely. A counterfeit pill mixed with alcohol isn't a benzodiazepine-plus-alcohol problem anymore. It may be an opioid-plus-alcohol problem, which can stop breathing quickly.

The rule is simple: **only take Xanax that was prescribed to you and dispensed by a pharmacy.** Never take a pill from a friend, a party, or an online seller. If you're with someone who took an unknown pill and becomes very hard to wake, call 911. If naloxone (Narcan) is available, it's reasonable to give it, because it can reverse opioids that may be hiding in the pill. It won't reverse alcohol or a real benzodiazepine, so it doesn't replace calling for help.

## Xanax, Alcohol, and Other Sedating Medicines

The same principle applies to anything else that slows the brain. Combining Xanax and alcohol with any of these adds more risk:

- **Opioid painkillers** such as oxycodone, hydrocodone, codeine, or tramadol. This is the combination with the FDA boxed warning, and adding alcohol makes it worse.
- **Sleep aids**, including prescription sleep drugs like zolpidem (Ambien) and over-the-counter "PM" products
- **Sedating antihistamines** such as diphenhydramine (Benadryl) and hydroxyzine. Our page on [Benadryl for a hangover](/never-hungover/benadryl-for-hangover) explains why these are a poor fit after drinking anyway.
- **Muscle relaxants**, some seizure medicines, and gabapentin or pregabalin
- **Cannabis**, which adds its own sedation and impairment

Even milder supplements deserve a mention. Melatonin is far less sedating than Xanax, but stacking sleep-promoting substances on a night of drinking isn't wise. See our guide to [melatonin and alcohol](/never-hungover/melatonin-and-alcohol). For a general look at how supplements interact with medicines, see our [DHM medication interactions and safety guide](/never-hungover/dhm-medication-interactions-safety-guide-2025).

## Withdrawal: Why You Shouldn't Stop Suddenly Either

Two facts about this combination surprise people:

- **Both alcohol and benzodiazepines can cause dangerous withdrawal.** After regular, heavy, or long-term use, suddenly stopping either one can cause tremors, sweating, severe anxiety, insomnia, hallucinations, and seizures.
- **They overlap.** Because they act on the same brake system, people who rely on both can have more complicated withdrawal.

This is why the label tells prescribers to taper benzodiazepines gradually rather than stopping them abruptly. If you take Xanax regularly and want to stop or cut back, or you drink heavily most days and want to stop, do it with a doctor's help, not cold turkey. That isn't about willpower. It's about safety.

For most social drinkers who take Xanax occasionally, withdrawal isn't the issue. The issue is simply not overlapping the two.

## Emergency Signs: When to Call 911

Combined Xanax and alcohol overdose can develop quietly. A person may seem to be "sleeping it off" while their breathing is getting dangerously slow. Don't leave someone alone to sleep if you're worried.

**Call 911 right away if someone who has taken Xanax (or an unknown pill) and alcohol:**

- Can't be woken up, or wakes only briefly and drifts off again
- Is breathing very slowly, shallowly, irregularly, or with long pauses, or is making snoring or gurgling sounds
- Has blue, gray, or pale lips, fingertips, or skin, or feels cold and clammy
- Has a very slow pulse
- Is having a seizure
- Is vomiting while drowsy or confused
- Is extremely confused, slurring badly, or can't stand

**While you wait for help:**

- Stay with them. Don't let them "sleep it off" alone.
- If they're breathing but unresponsive, roll them onto their side (the recovery position) so they won't choke if they vomit.
- Don't give them coffee, a cold shower, or more pills. These don't speed recovery.
- If opioids or a counterfeit pill could be involved and you have naloxone, give it.
- Tell emergency responders exactly what was taken, how much, and when, if you know. Bring the pill bottle if there is one.

Many US states have **Good Samaritan laws** that offer some legal protection to people who call for help during an overdose. Fear of trouble should never stop anyone from calling.

For non-emergency questions, like whether a past dose and a past drink could still interact, call your pharmacist or Poison Control at **1-800-222-1222** (US).

## Who Should Be Especially Careful

The risk is higher if you:

- Are **over 65**, since older adults tend to clear alprazolam more slowly and are more prone to falls and confusion
- Have **sleep apnea, COPD, or other breathing problems**
- Have **liver disease**
- Take **opioids** or any other sedating medicine
- Take **XR (extended-release)** Xanax or take it on a daily schedule
- Have a personal or family history of **substance use problems**
- Are **pregnant** or breastfeeding

If any of these describe you, the "talk to your prescriber" advice isn't a formality. Ask directly: "What should I do about alcohol while I'm on this?"

## Where DHM Fits In, and Where It Doesn't

We cover DHM (dihydromyricetin) a lot on this site, so it's worth being clear about it here.

DHM is a plant compound studied for its effects on alcohol. One of the best-known animal studies, published in the *Journal of Neuroscience* in 2012, found that DHM reduced signs of alcohol intoxication in rats and appeared to work partly through **GABA-A receptors**, the same receptors Xanax and alcohol act on. Human evidence is still limited.

That has two honest consequences:

1. **DHM is not a way to make Xanax and alcohol safe together.** There is no good evidence that any supplement prevents the breathing and sedation risks described above. Nothing changes the core rule: don't combine them.
2. **Don't add DHM to Xanax without asking.** Because DHM seems to act at the same receptor system in animal studies, and its interaction with benzodiazepines in people hasn't been studied, check with your prescriber or pharmacist before taking DHM if you take Xanax or any other benzodiazepine.

For social drinkers who **aren't** taking Xanax or other sedating medicines, DHM is one of the supplements people use alongside the basics of drinking less, eating, and staying hydrated. Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers the research and typical use, and our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) covers the habits with the best evidence.

## The Bottom Line

- Xanax and alcohol both act on the brain's GABA "brake" system. Together they can amplify each other, slowing breathing and causing heavy sedation, blackouts, coma, or death.
- There is no known safe amount of alcohol with Xanax. The prescribing information tells patients to avoid alcohol.
- Xanax stays in your system long after the calm wears off, so "timing it" is unreliable. Ask your prescriber how to handle alcohol before it comes up.
- Don't use Xanax for hangover anxiety, and never take a Xanax that didn't come from a pharmacy.
- Don't stop regular Xanax or heavy daily drinking abruptly. Do it with a doctor.
- If someone who mixed them is hard to wake or breathing slowly, call 911 and stay with them.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Is it safe to drink alcohol while taking Xanax?**

No. Xanax (alprazolam) and alcohol both slow the brain through the same GABA system, and together they can cause heavy sedation, blackouts, and dangerously slow breathing. There is no amount of alcohol known to be safe with Xanax, and the prescribing information tells patients to avoid alcohol. Talk to your prescriber about how to handle alcohol before it comes up.

**How long after taking Xanax can I drink alcohol?**

There is no official waiting period that applies to everyone. Immediate-release alprazolam has an average half-life of around 11 hours in healthy adults, with wide variation, so a meaningful amount can stay in your system into the next day even after the calming effect fades. Older adults, people with liver disease, and people on certain other medicines clear it more slowly. Ask your prescriber or pharmacist rather than guessing.

**Can I take Xanax for a hangover or hangover anxiety?**

It's a bad idea. Alcohol may still be in your blood the morning after, so you'd be combining the two. Hangover anxiety is partly a rebound from alcohol itself, and covering it with another depressant can build a risky pattern. In people who drink heavily every day, shakiness and anxiety can also be early alcohol withdrawal, which needs a doctor rather than self-treatment.

**What happens if you mix Xanax and alcohol?**

Effects range from strong drowsiness, poor coordination, slurred speech, and memory gaps to, at higher amounts, very slow or stopped breathing, choking on vomit, coma, and death. How strongly the two combine is hard to predict and depends on dose, timing, body size, food, and any other sedating substances involved.

**What are the signs of a Xanax and alcohol overdose?**

Call 911 if someone can't be woken, is breathing very slowly, shallowly, or with long pauses, has blue or gray lips or fingertips, has a very slow pulse, is having a seizure, or is vomiting while drowsy or confused. Stay with them, roll them onto their side if they're breathing but unresponsive, and give naloxone if opioids or a counterfeit pill could be involved.

**Is the Xanax and alcohol warning an FDA boxed warning?**

Xanax carries an FDA boxed warning, the agency's strongest, about combining benzodiazepines with opioids and about the risks of abuse, misuse, addiction, dependence, and withdrawal. Alcohol is covered in the label's warnings about other central nervous system depressants, which tell patients to avoid alcohol. The reasoning is the same as for opioids: two substances that slow breathing are more dangerous together.

**Are other benzodiazepines like Ativan, Valium, or Klonopin safe with alcohol?**

No. Lorazepam (Ativan), diazepam (Valium), clonazepam (Klonopin), and other benzodiazepines act on the same GABA-A receptor as alprazolam and carry the same core risk with alcohol: added sedation, memory loss, and slowed breathing. Some last even longer in the body than Xanax. Ask your prescriber about alcohol for whichever one you take.

**Can I take DHM if I'm on Xanax?**

Check with your prescriber or pharmacist first. In animal studies DHM appears to act partly at GABA-A receptors, the same system Xanax works on, and its interaction with benzodiazepines in people hasn't been studied. There is also no good evidence that DHM or any supplement makes it safe to combine Xanax and alcohol.
